summary: Specifies a second version of Robust Header Compression profiles for RTP, UDP, IP, ESP and UDP-Lite headers. It simplifies the rules and adds robustness against loss and reordering. It supersedes the earlier profiles in RFC 3095, RFC 3843 and RFC 4019 without making them obsolete. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary:
Every packet carries a header, and in most traffic those headers repeat almost exactly from one packet to the next. Header compression exploits that by sending only what changed.

This document defines a second generation of the ROHC compression profiles. It simplifies the rules an implementation has to follow, and it lets the sender and the receiver cope with packets that arrive late or go missing, which the earlier profiles could not do.

questions: how does rohc handle packet reordering
what is the rohcv2 decompressor state machine
subtitle: A second version of the ROHC header compression profiles, simpler to implement and tolerant of lost and reordered packets.

tldr.problem: Packet headers carry many bytes that repeat from packet to packet, so the ROHC framework compresses them. The first set of profiles needed several operating modes and assumed the link never reordered packets, which made them hard to implement and fragile on real links.
tldr.mechanism: ROHCv2 keeps the same idea but simplifies the rules: the compressor sends a full Initialization and Refresh header first, then smaller Compressed headers, and it keeps sending a field until it is confident the other end received it. A three-state decompressor checks every header with a CRC and falls back to bigger headers when a check fails.
tldr.outcome: The profiles handle a limited amount of loss and reordering as part of the compression itself, can compress any number of nested IP headers, and define feedback formats with a mandatory CRC. They supersede the profile definitions in RFC 3095, RFC 3843 and RFC 4019 without making those documents obsolete.

today: RFC 5225 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It supersedes the profile definitions in RFC 3095, RFC 3843 and RFC 4019 without making those documents obsolete, and it depends on the ROHC framework in RFC 4995.

sections.title: What ROHCv2 Defines
sections.content:
ROHC is a header compression framework with profiles for different protocol stacks, first documented in RFC 3095 together with profiles for RTP/UDP/IP, UDP/IP, IP and ESP/IP headers. Additional profiles for IP headers were later specified in RFC 3843, and for UDP-Lite headers in RFC 4019.

This document defines an updated version of each of those profiles. The definitions depend on the ROHC framework as found in RFC 4995, which the RFC calls required reading, and the formal notation used to write the header formats is defined in RFC 4997.

The profiles defined here are RTP/UDP/IP as profile 0x0101, UDP/IP as 0x0102, ESP/IP as 0x0103, IP as 0x0104, RTP/UDP-Lite/IP as 0x0107 and UDP-Lite/IP as 0x0108. Each of them can also compress the AH, GRE, MINE, IPv6 Destination Options, IPv6 Hop-by-hop Options and IPv6 Routing extension headers.

The ROHCv2 profiles simplify the rules and algorithms that govern the behaviour of the compression endpoints. They define robustness mechanisms that a compressor implementation may use to raise the probability of successful decompression when packets are lost or reordered on the ROHC channel, and they define their own set of header formats using the ROHC formal notation.
sections.plainLanguage:
ROHC is a set of rules for shrinking packet headers. This document replaces the first set of rules with a simpler one, and it adds rules for coping with packets that get lost or arrive out of order.

Six profiles are defined, one for each combination of headers they compress: RTP over UDP over IP, UDP over IP, ESP over IP, plain IP, RTP over UDP-Lite over IP, and UDP-Lite over IP.

sections.title: Which Header Fields Are Hard to Compress
sections.content:
Header compression is possible because there is a lot of redundancy between the field values in the headers of a packet, especially between the headers of consecutive packets. Appendix A of the RFC classifies every field that the profiles compress and concludes that most of them can be compressed away, since they never or seldom change.

A small number of fields need more sophisticated mechanisms: the IPv4 Identification field, IP-ID, which is 16 bits; the ESP Sequence Number, 32 bits; the UDP Checksum, 16 bits; the UDP-Lite Checksum, 16 bits; the UDP-Lite Checksum Coverage, 16 bits; the RTP Marker bit, 1 bit; the RTP Sequence Number, 16 bits; and the RTP Timestamp, 32 bits.

Two correlations do most of the remaining work. The RTP Timestamp usually tracks the RTP Sequence Number, which increases by one for each packet an RTP source emits, so the timestamp can be predicted once the increment is known. The RTP M-bit is expected to have the same value most of the time, but it has to be communicated explicitly on occasion. A similar correlation is often seen between the IPv4 Identifier field and the master sequence number used for compression.

Some fields cannot be compressed away at all. The UDP Checksum cannot be inferred or recalculated at the receiving end without breaking its end-to-end properties, so it is sent as-is when it is enabled, and it is mandatory with IPv6. The same applies to the UDP-Lite Checksum, which is mandatory with both IPv4 and IPv6, while the UDP-Lite Checksum Coverage may in some cases be compressible.
sections.plainLanguage: Most header fields stay the same from one packet to the next, so they can be left out of the compressed packet and remembered by the receiver instead. Only a few fields change in ways that need special handling, such as the sequence number and timestamp that carry real-time media.

sections.title: What Changes Compared With the RFC 3095 Profiles
sections.content:
The ROHCv2 profiles can achieve compression efficiency and robustness that are both at least equivalent to the RFC 3095 profiles when used under the same operating conditions. The size and bit layout of the smallest compressed header, the U/O-0 format in RFC 3095 and pt_0_crc3 in ROHCv2, are identical.

The differences are these.

  • Tolerance to reordering. The RFC 3095 profiles require the channel between compressor and decompressor to provide in-order delivery. ROHCv2 can handle a limited amount of reordering after the compression point as part of the compression algorithm itself, which also makes it possible to handle prelink reordering more efficiently.
  • Operational logic. The RFC 3095 profiles define multiple operational modes, each with different updating logic and compressed header formats. ROHCv2 profiles operate unidirectionally until feedback is first received for a context, and bidirectionally from that point on; the formats are independent of which operational logic is used.
  • IP extension headers. RFC 3095 compresses IP extension headers using list compression. ROHCv2 treats extension headers in the same manner as other protocol headers, using the chaining mechanism, so it assumes that extension headers are not added or removed during the lifetime of a context.
  • IP encapsulation. RFC 3095 can compress at most two levels of IP headers. ROHCv2 can compress an arbitrary number of IP headers.
  • List compression. ROHCv2 profiles do not support reference-based list compression.
  • Robustness and repairs. ROHCv2 profiles do not define a format for the IR-DYN packet. Each profile instead defines a compressed header that can be used to perform a more robust context repair using a 7-bit CRC verification. Only the IR header can change the association between a context identifier and the profile it uses.
  • Feedback. ROHCv2 profiles mandate a CRC in the format of the FEEDBACK-2, while this is optional in RFC 3095, and they use a different set of feedback options.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier profiles had several separate operating modes and needed the link to deliver packets in order. This version has one way of working, and the receiver can tell from each packet whether it was decoded correctly, so a lost or late packet no longer breaks the whole flow.

sections.title: How the Compressor Decides What to Send
sections.content:
Header compression can be characterised as the interaction of a compressor with a decompressor state machine, one per context. The compressor's responsibility is to convey the information needed to successfully decompress a packet, based on a certain confidence regarding the state of the decompressor context. That confidence is obtained from the frequency and the type of information the compressor sends when updating the decompressor context, and optionally from feedback messages received from the decompressor.

The compressor always uses the optimistic approach when it performs context updates. It normally repeats the same type of update until it is fairly confident that the decompressor has successfully received the information. If field X in the uncompressed header changes value, the compressor uses a header type that contains an encoding of field X until it has gained confidence that the decompressor has received at least one packet containing the new value for X, normally selecting the compressed format with the smallest header that can convey the change. How many repetitions are needed depends on the packet loss and out-of-order delivery characteristics of the link, and the number is left to implementors to decide.

Two tradeoffs follow. For fields encoded with least significant bits, the interpretation interval offset of the sliding window sets an upper limit on the reordering depth the encoding can absorb, and the same window is what gives the encoding its tolerance of consecutive losses. The offset is typically bound to the number of least-significant-bit compressed bits in the header format, so it grows as more bits are transmitted. For seldom changing fields, the optimistic approach sets the limit on reordering that can be handled, so there is a tradeoff between compression efficiency and robustness. Compressor implementations should adjust their strategy to match both the packet loss and the reordering characteristics of the link.

Operation starts unidirectionally. The compressor assumes the decompressor has no useful information about the new flow and sends Initialization and Refresh packets. It does not expect feedback for the flow until feedback first arrives, at which point it may assume the decompressor will continue to send feedback in order to repair its context when necessary; this is called bidirectional operation. Because the decompressor may not have received enough information to decompress the packets correctly, the compressor SHOULD periodically send IR packets until the feedback channel is established. Once it is established, the periodic refreshes become superfluous and the compressor can rely entirely on the optimistic approach and on feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender never knows for certain whether a packet arrived. So it keeps repeating an update until it is reasonably sure the receiver got it, and only then switches to sending smaller packets. The receiver's replies, once they start, let the sender do this more accurately.

sections.title: The Decompressor and Its Feedback
sections.content:
The decompressor normally uses the last received and successfully validated or verified header as the reference for future decompression. It verifies the outcome of every decompression attempt with the CRC present in the compressed header, updates its context when the attempt succeeds, and requests context repairs through feedback once it has started using feedback.

Its operation is a state machine with three states. No Context (NC) means no valid context has been established yet, and in that state only packets carrying sufficient information on the static fields, that is IR packets, can be decompressed. The decompressor moves to Full Context when the CRC-8 validation of an IR header succeeds, and it should send a STATIC-NACK if it receives a packet of a type other than IR, or an IR header that fails CRC-8 validation.

Repair Context (RC) means the decompressor has successfully decompressed packets for this context but does not have confidence that the entire context is valid. Only headers covered by an 8-bit CRC, or CO headers carrying a 7-bit CRC, can be decompressed in this state. The decompressor moves up to Full Context when the CRC verification succeeds for a CO header carrying a 7-bit CRC or when validation of an 8-bit CRC in an IR header succeeds, and it moves back to No Context if it assumes static context damage.

In Full Context (FC) the decompressor assumes that its entire context is valid, and decompression can be attempted regardless of the type of packet received. It moves back to Repair Context if it assumes context damage, and directly to No Context if it assumes static context damage.

Context damage means the decompressor will not attempt decompression of a CO header that carries only a 3-bit CRC, and will attempt only IR headers or CO headers protected by a 7-bit CRC. Static context damage means it refrains from attempting decompression of any type of header other than the IR header. How these assumptions are made is left to implementations, and can be based on the residual error rate.

Feedback uses the three message types of the ROHC framework: ACKs, NACKs and STATIC-NACKs. The decompressor should send a NACK when it assumes context damage and a STATIC-NACK when it assumes static context damage. It is not strictly expected to send ACK feedback upon successful decompression, other than to improve compression efficiency, and it should limit the rate at which it sends feedback and avoid sending unnecessary duplicates of the same type.

The feedback formats are defined in Section 6.9. A FEEDBACK-1 carries the eight least significant bits of the master sequence number and is always an ACK. A FEEDBACK-2 adds an acknowledgement type, where 0 is ACK, 1 is NACK and 2 is STATIC-NACK, and always carries an 8-bit CRC that the compressor MUST verify, discarding the feedback element if the computed value differs. Four options are defined. REJECT tells the compressor that the decompressor does not have sufficient resources, and the compressor MUST stop compressing the packet flow. ACKNUMBER-NOT-VALID says the Acknowledgment Number field cannot be used to find the corresponding sent header. CONTEXT_MEMORY tells the compressor the decompressor lacks memory for the context as the flow is currently compressed. CLOCK_RESOLUTION carries the decompressor's clock resolution in milliseconds; the smallest value that can be indicated is 1 millisecond, and the value zero means the decompressor cannot do timer-based compression of the RTP Timestamp.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver keeps one of three levels of confidence. With no context it can only read full headers. With a damaged context it can read almost anything but checks harder. With a full context it reads everything and trusts its records, checking each packet with a small checksum. If a check fails, the receiver falls back to a more cautious level and tells the sender.

sections.title: The Control Fields
sections.content:
ROHCv2 defines a number of control fields that the decompressor uses in its interpretation of the header formats it receives from the compressor.

The Master Sequence Number (MSN) is either taken from a field that already exists in one of the headers being compressed, such as the RTP sequence number, or created by the compressor. There is one MSN space per context and one MSN field in every ROHCv2 header: the MSN is sent in full in IR headers, while it can be least-significant-bit encoded within CO header formats. It has two functions: telling apart reference headers when feedback data arrives, and inferring the value of incrementing fields such as the IPv4 Identifier. For the profiles where the compressor creates it, 0x0102, 0x0104 and 0x0108, the compressor initialises the MSN to a random value when the context is first created or when the profile associated with a context changes, and its value SHOULD be incremented by one for each packet the compressor sends for that context.

The reorder_ratio control field says how much reordering is handled by the least-significant-bit encoding of the MSN, so the compressor can adjust the balance between robustness to reordering and robustness to consecutive losses on a link whose reordering characteristics change.

The IP-ID behavior control field records whether the IPv4 Identification field is sequential in network byte order, sequential byte-swapped, random or constant. There is one such control field per IP header, and the one for the innermost IP header determines which set of header formats is used. When more than one level of IP headers is compressed, ROHCv2 profiles MUST NOT assign a sequential behaviour to any IP-ID except the one in the innermost header, so a compressor MUST assign either the constant zero or the random behaviour to tunnelling headers.

Two more control fields relate to timing. ts_stride is the expected increase in the RTP timestamp between consecutive RTP sequence numbers, and its default value is 160. time_stride is the time interval equivalent to one ts_stride, and when timer-based compression is used it should be set to the expected difference in arrival time between consecutive RTP packets. The coverage_behavior control field says how the checksum coverage field of the UDP-Lite header is compressed, using irregular, static or inferred encoding.

Control fields are protected by a 3-bit CRC, the CRC-3, which is present in the header format for the co_common and co_repair header types. The decompressor MUST always validate the integrity of the control fields covered by this CRC when processing those formats, and failure to validate them should be considered a decompression failure. If the decompression attempt can be verified using either the CRC-3 or the CRC-7 calculated over the uncompressed header, the decompressor MAY still forward the header, because the protected control fields are not always used to decompress the header that updates their value.

Verification itself is spelled out separately. The decompressor MUST always validate the IR header using the 8-bit CRC carried within it, and if it cannot be validated the context MUST NOT be updated and the header MUST NOT be delivered to upper layers. It MUST always verify a CO header using the CRC carried within it, and if the reconstructed header fails verification the context updates MUST NOT be performed. A packet whose decompression attempt cannot be verified MUST NOT be delivered to upper layers.
sections.plainLanguage: A few extra values travel with the compressed header because the receiver cannot work them out for itself. The most important is a master sequence number, which stands in for the packet numbering of whichever protocol is being compressed. Others say how much reordering to expect and how the address field is numbered.

sections.title: The IR and CO Header Formats
sections.content:
ROHCv2 profiles use two header types: the Initialization and Refresh (IR) header type, and the Compressed (CO) header type.

The IR header format uses the structure of the ROHC IR header as defined in Section 5.2.2.1 of RFC 4995, and communicates the static part and the dynamic part of the context. It carries an optional Add-CID octet for small context identifiers, an IR type octet whose bits are 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 1, 0 to 2 octets of context identifier for large ones, one octet of profile, one octet of CRC, and then the static chain and the dynamic chain, both of variable length. The CRC is an 8-bit CRC over the entire IR header, including any context identifier fields and up until the end of the dynamic chain.

The CO header type defines a number of formats. There are two sets of base header formats for each profile: one set for headers where the innermost IP header contains a sequential IP-ID, either network byte order or byte-swapped, and one set for headers without a sequential IP-ID. Formats in the sequential set include 'seq' in their name, and formats in the other set include 'rnd'.

Four formats are common to both sets. co_common can be used to update the context when the established change pattern of a dynamic field changes; it contains a set of flags that indicate what fields are present, its size varies accordingly, and it is protected by a 7-bit CRC. co_repair can be used to update the context of all the dynamic fields by conveying their uncompressed value, which is what is needed when context damage is assumed and a repair is performed; it is also protected by a 7-bit CRC. pt_0_crc3 conveys only the MSN, so it can update only the MSN and the fields derived from it, such as the IP-ID and the RTP Timestamp, and it is protected by a 3-bit CRC. pt_0_crc7 has the same properties but is protected by a 7-bit CRC and contains a larger amount of least-significant-bit MSN bits, which makes it useful where a high amount of reordering or a high residual error rate can occur.

Other formats exist for the profiles that compress RTP. pt_1_rnd conveys changes to the MSN and the RTP Marker bit and can update the RTP timestamp using scaled timestamp encoding. pt_1_seq_id conveys changes to the MSN and the IP-ID. pt_1_seq_ts conveys changes to the MSN and the Marker bit and can update the RTP Timestamp using scaled timestamp encoding. pt_2_rnd conveys changes to the MSN, the Marker bit and the RTP Timestamp. pt_2_seq_id conveys changes to the MSN and the IP-ID, and pt_2_seq_ts conveys changes to the MSN and the Marker bit and can update the RTP Timestamp using scaled timestamp encoding. pt_2_seq_both conveys changes to both the RTP Timestamp and the IP-ID, in addition to the MSN and the Marker bit. All of these are protected by a 3-bit or a 7-bit CRC, as their names indicate.

Fields are grouped into chains. The static chain holds the fields that rarely change, one item for each header of the chain of protocol headers being compressed, starting from the outermost IP header, and it is used only in the IR header format. The dynamic chain holds the fields that change from packet to packet and is used in the IR and co_repair formats. The irregular chain holds the fields whose behaviour does not fit a pattern, and is used in all CO headers except co_repair. Chaining is done by appending an item for each header in the order the headers appear in the uncompressed packet.
sections.plainLanguage: A compressed packet starts with a big header that carries everything, and then shrinks. The big one is the IR header. The small ones are CO headers, and each kind of CO header says what it can update and how well it is checked: a 3-bit check for the smallest headers and a 7-bit check for the ones that change more context.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Impairments such as bit errors on the received compressed headers, missing packets, and reordering between packets could cause the header decompressor to reconstitute erroneous packets, that is, packets that do not match the original packet but still have a valid IP, UDP or UDP-Lite and RTP header, and possibly also a valid UDP or UDP-Lite checksum.

The header compression profiles defined here use an internal checksum for verification of reconstructed headers. This reduces the probability that a header decompressor delivers erroneous packets to upper layers without the error being noticed. In particular, the probability that consecutive erroneous packets are not detected by the internal checksum is close to zero.

This small but non-zero probability remains unchanged when integrity protection is applied after compression and verified before decompression, in the case where an attacker could discard or reorder packets between the compression endpoints.

The impairments mentioned above could also be caused by a malfunctioning or malicious header compressor. Such corruption may be detected with end-to-end integrity mechanisms that will not be affected by the compression, and the internal checksum can also be useful against a malfunctioning compressor.

Denial-of-service attacks are possible if an intruder can introduce bogus IR or FEEDBACK packets onto the link and thereby cause compression efficiency to be reduced. However, an intruder having the ability to inject arbitrary packets at the link layer in this manner raises additional security issues that dwarf those related to the use of header compression.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression can go wrong: a damaged or lost packet can make the receiver build a header that looks valid but is not the original. The profiles guard against this with a small checksum on every compressed header, so two wrong headers in a row passing the check is very unlikely. The RFC also notes that the real risk is an attacker injecting packets, which is a bigger problem than header compression itself.
